snippet.title: The Chrysler Family: The Secret Gay Heir, The Nazi King, and Fake Picassos (Documentary)
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore how Walter P. Chrysler Sr. — a railroad mechanic from Wamego, Kansas — built America's third-largest automaker and the world's tallest building, then watched the entire fortune unravel across his four children in a single generation.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

Thelma Chrysler Foy lived at 740 Park Avenue, collected 18th-century French furniture, and died of leukemia at 54. Her estate was auctioned at Parke-Bernet in 1959 across 770 lots.

Bernice Chrysler Garbisch married a West Point football star turned Nazi-sympathizing executive and assembled the largest private collection of American folk art ever donated to a museum. She died by suicide at Pokety the same day her husband Edgar died of a stroke in 1979.

Jack Chrysler died of a heart attack at 46 in 1958, leaving a young wife and two minor children with a portfolio of brokerage interests and a residual share of the Chrysler Building.

Walter P. Chrysler Jr. spent his life and his inheritance on roughly 3,800 paintings — including 347 Picassos, 90 of which the Art Dealers Association of America publicly declared fakes in 1962. His alleged relationship with the abdicated Edward, Duke of Windsor was reported decades later by historian Andrew Lownie.

The Chrysler Building left the family in 1953. The corporation was bailed out by Congress in 1979, sold to Daimler-Benz in 1998, and is now part of Stellantis. The spire is still there.

snippet.title: When Two Brothers From Brooklyn Bought CBS and the New York Giants: The Tisch Family
snippet.description:
In 1946, a 23-year-old from Brooklyn spotted a listing in the New York Times for a rundown 300-room resort in New Jersey called Laurel-in-the-Pines. He bought it for $125,000 — largely his parents' savings — cut costs, imported three reindeer from Finland to pull sleighs in the snow, and turned a profit immediately. When he died fifty-seven years later, the empire he and his brother had built from that single hotel included a Fortune 500 conglomerate, a television network they sold for $5.4 billion, fifty percent of the New York Giants, and a philanthropic legacy that put the family name on a hospital, an arts school, and museum galleries across New York City. Their formula never changed: buy what others are fleeing, cut what others are padding, and wait.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

Laurence Alan Tisch was born March 5, 1923 in Brooklyn. His younger brother Preston Robert "Bob" Tisch was born April 29, 1926 in the same Bensonhurst neighborhood — the sons of Abraham "Al" Tisch and Sayde Brenner, children of immigrants from Ukraine and Poland.

Larry graduated cum laude from NYU at eighteen and earned a master's in industrial management from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania — all by the age of twenty. Bob attended Bucknell, served in the U.S. Army during World War Two, and earned a bachelor's degree in economics from the University of Michigan.

Larry was the financial architect — quiet, numbers-obsessed, allergic to glamour. Bob was the gregarious front man, skilled at relationships and operational management. The complementary partnership would define Loews Corporation's culture for decades.

In 1946, Larry spotted the Laurel-in-the-Pines listing and bought the rundown New Jersey resort with $125,000 in family capital. Two years later Bob joined as a full partner. The brothers added a swimming pool, improved food service, and imported the Finnish reindeer.

Over the next decade they acquired a dozen hotels across New Jersey, Atlantic City, and the Catskills. In 1956 they built the Americana at Bal Harbour, Florida for $17 million of their own money. In 1961, the 800-room Summit Hotel in midtown Manhattan — the first hotel built in the city in thirty years. In 1962, the 50-story Americana in Times Square, the world's tallest hotel upon completion.

In 1959, the Tisch brothers purchased a controlling interest in Loew's Theatres from MGM for roughly $17 million — an acquisition made possible by the 1948 Paramount Decrees that forced studios to divest their theater chains. Most investors saw declining attendance. The Tisches saw prime urban real estate dressed up as cinemas.

In 1968, Loews acquired Lorillard Tobacco — owner of Newport, Kent, and True — when most institutional investors were avoiding tobacco stocks. In 1974, Larry executed his most spectacular value investment: the acquisition of CNA Financial, a major insurance firm teetering on bankruptcy, for approximately $206 million for an 83% stake. By 2025, the holding was valued at approximately $10.8 billion.

Larry toured CNA's grandiose headquarters, found a chairman's suite with a marble staircase leading to a private dining room, closed it, and told the staff the marble staircase was everything they needed to know about why the company had nearly failed.

In 1985, CBS attracted predators. Ted Turner launched a hostile bid totaling nearly $3 billion. Senator Jesse Helms organized Fairness in Media. CEO Thomas Wyman invited Larry Tisch in as a white knight. Larry purchased shares until Loews held 24.9% at a cost of approximately $800 million, then allied with 84-year-old founder William S. Paley.

On September 10, 1986, Wyman resigned. Tisch became acting chief executive. He laid off 230 CBS News employees, closed three overseas bureaus, slashed $30 million from the news budget, and shed roughly 1,200 of the network's 15,500 employees. Dan Rather publicly challenged him, evoking Edward R. Murrow.

CBS Records — the world's largest record label, owner of Michael Jackson's catalog — was sold to Sony in November 1987 for $2 billion, nearly double Sony's initial offer. CBS Magazines were sold for $650 million. He recruited David Letterman from NBC for $14 million annually. He lost the NFC rights in 1993 because he refused to bid above the previous contract — Fox, led by Rupert Murdoch, outbid CBS by more than $1.29 billion. In August 1995, Westinghouse paid $5.4 billion in cash for CBS.

In February 1991, days after the Giants beat Buffalo in Super Bowl XXV, Bob Tisch purchased fifty percent of the New York Giants from Tim Mara — who was suffering from Hodgkin's disease — for between $60 and $80 million.

snippet.title: The House of Lancaster - The Red Rose of England Documentary
snippet.description:
Discover the ultimate story of royal power and wealth! This video charts the 750-year history of the Lancastrian legacy, from its origins as a medieval earldom to its status today.

We begin in 1267, when the title of Earl of Lancaster was first granted. Trace the rapid accumulation of power that led to the creation of the Dukedom for Henry of Grosmont in 1351. snippet.title: The Dynasty Who Built a $2 Billion Empire from a Single Gas Pump and Never Went Public: Buc-ee's
snippet.description:
Every gas station in America is terrible — and every gas station in America is profitable, because drivers have no better option. One man asked the simplest question in business: what if someone just made a better one? Forty-four years later, the answer is approximately 69 locations, two Guinness World Records, an estimated $2 billion valuation, and a 50/50 partnership that has never sold a single share.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

Buc-ee's ranked first among all U.S. convenience retailers in the 2025 dunnhumby Convenience Retailer Preference Index, scoring seventeen points ahead of second-place Sheetz — with approximately 69 locations against competitors operating over a thousand each.

Arch "Beaver" Aplin III graduated from Texas A&M in 1980 with a construction science degree and a plan to build skyscrapers. He noticed something on his daily commute that most people had stopped seeing — every gas station was dirty, unfriendly, and poorly stocked, yet every one was profitable.

His childhood nickname came from Bucky the Beaver, the Ipana toothpaste mascot. Combined with his Labrador Retriever's name, Buck, he had a brand and a mascot.

On July 28, 1982, Buc-ee's Number One opened at 899 Oyster Creek Drive in Lake Jackson, Texas — a 3,000-square-foot store with a handful of gas pumps.

His partner Don Wasek brought operational discipline. The two shared a single desk for the first three years. Their 50/50 split has lasted 44 years without a public disagreement.

The Luling decision in 2003 changed everything — a 10,764-square-foot "family travel center" off I-10. Before Luling, chain sales were $63 million. By 2006, they had tripled to $202 million. By 2015, $959 million.

The average Buc-ee's today spans 50,000 to 75,000 square feet with 80 to 120 fuel pumps — twenty to thirty times the industry standard. The Luling replacement opened in June 2024 at 75,593 square feet, the world's largest convenience store.

For the first 37 years, Buc-ee's never opened a single store outside Texas. The first out-of-state location opened in Alabama in 2019. Expansion has since reached more than a dozen states with seven more confirmed.

Every location is financed through bank debt, never equity. The company has never taken venture capital, never entertained a private equity partner, and has no plans to go public.

The $2 billion empire belongs entirely to two men who shared a desk, split the equity 50/50, and proved that obsessive execution in the most unglamorous business on earth can be worth more than disruption.

In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the 125-year arc of the Annenberg dynasty — a Prussian-Jewish immigrant family that arrived in America through Castle Garden in 1885 with no money, built one of the most powerful and violent newspaper-distribution empires of the early twentieth century through bloody Chicago circulation wars, a national race-wire monopoly serving bookmakers in 44 states, and personal friendships with Lucky Luciano and Meyer Lansky, and then spent the next sixty years converting that fortune into Presidential Medals, a billion-dollar art collection at the Metropolitan Museum, a $500 million reform of American public schools, a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II, and more than $4 billion in philanthropy across three generations — the most extraordinary act of reputation laundering in American history.

————————————————————————————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

————————————————————————————————————————

Moses "Moe" Annenberg was born in 1877 in a Prussian village called Kallwischken, where a neighboring blacksmith dropped a ham hock into the family well to contaminate the water of the only observant Jewish family on the road — Moe's first conscious memory of antisemitism, and a lesson in territorial aggression that would define his American career.

The family arrived in America through Castle Garden in 1885, chosen deliberately over Ellis Island because Castle Garden did not charge the $25 landing fee that would have resulted in immediate deportation — and settled on Maxwell Street in Chicago, the immigrant slum the Chicago Tribune later called "Bloody Maxwell" and described as producing murderers, robbers, and thieves at a rate exceeding any similar district on Earth.

Moe dropped out of school at twelve, sold newspapers alongside his brother Max, and entered William Randolph Hearst's circulation army during the Chicago newspaper wars of 1910 to 1912 — a series of street battles between Hearst and Tribune distribution gangs that left 27 dead newsboys, drivers, and circulation men in the streets of Chicago.

The Annenberg brothers ran the Hearst side of the war and emerged on top — and Moe spent the next two decades consolidating control over American horse-racing wire services through the General News Bureau and ultimately the Nationwide News Service, the race wire that became the single most valuable piece of organized-crime infrastructure in America, serving bookmakers in 44 states.

Moe paid the Capone Syndicate roughly $1 million a year in protection money, was personally friendly with Lucky Luciano — who once described him as "my kind of guy" — and operated in the gray zone where legitimate publishing and organized crime were indistinguishable, while simultaneously running the Philadelphia Inquirer, Daily Racing Form, and a chain of scandal publications that effectively functioned as blackmail leverage against the wealthy.

In 1939, the federal government indicted Moe on tax-evasion charges before Judge James H. Wilkerson — the same judge who had convicted Al Capone — and named his son Walter as a co-defendant.

Moe pleaded guilty, agreed to prison and $9.5 million in taxes and penalties, and in exchange all charges against Walter were dropped — the deal was brutal in its personal cost, and Moe died of a brain tumor 39 days after his release from Lewisburg Federal Prison in 1942.

Walter Annenberg inherited the fortune at 34, deeply in debt, shadowed by scandal, and carrying the specific psychological burden of a man who had escaped prison only because his father had taken the sentence for him — he later said the experience felt "like being lashed by a whip."

Over the next sixty years, Walter spent the family fortune on the systematic project of reputation conversion: launching TV Guide in 1953 (which became one of the most profitable magazines in American publishing history), launching Seventeen, expanding the Daily Racing Form into a national franchise, and ultimately selling Triangle Publications to Rupert Murdoch in 1988 for $3 billion.

In 1969, Richard Nixon appointed Walter U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James's — a tenure that began with a televised gaffe at his credentials presentation so excruciating it became a national joke in Britain, and ended with Queen Elizabeth II making him an Honorary Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire.

In February 1983, the Queen and Prince Philip arrived at Sunnylands — the Annenbergs' 200-acre mid-century-modern estate in Rancho Mirage, California — for a private luncheon during a ten-day American tour, one of the rare occasions she ever visited a private home in the United States.

snippet.title: The forgotten Civil War roots of Memorial Day
snippet.description:
A federal holiday since 1971, the roots of Memorial Day go back over a century prior, to the end of the Civil War.

After the burial of many Union and Confederate soldiers, "decoration day" rituals began to spring up, which included placing fresh flowers on soldiers' graves.

One of the earliest known celebrations took place in Charleston, South Carolina on May 1, 1865, when the city's freed Black residents organized a proper burial for hundreds of Union soldiers who had died in a Confederate prison, followed by a parade to honor their memory.

In the spring of 1868, General John Logan officially designated May 30th "for the purpose of strewing flowers or otherwise decorating the graves of comrades who died in the defense of their country," and Memorial Day as we know it today was established.

Discover the political and social changes wrought by the conflict's unprecedented death toll in DEATH AND THE CIVIL WAR, now streaming on the PBS Documentaries Prime Video Channel → https://to.pbs.org/43s0B37

snippet.title: The Man Warren Buffett Called the Greatest Businessman He Ever Knew The Enterprise Rent A Car Saga
snippet.description:
In the central Pacific during the final 18 months of the Second World War, a Navy fighter pilot from St. Louis was flying F6F Hellcat aircraft off the deck of a Yorktown-class aircraft carrier called the USS Enterprise. His name was Jack C. Taylor, and he flew combat missions in the squadron rotation that carried American naval aviation to the doorstep of the Japanese home islands by the summer of 1945. When the war ended, Jack Taylor came home with a Navy Air Medal and no clear sense of what a Midwestern aviator without a college degree was supposed to do for a living. He took a job selling Cadillacs at a St. Louis dealership, and spent the next 11 years on the showroom floor. In 1957, with seven cars in the basement of the dealership and a 25 percent stake personally guaranteed by his employer, he founded a small leasing operation called Executive Leasing. Twelve years later, in 1969, he renamed the company after the aircraft carrier he had flown off in the Pacific.

In this in-depth episode of Old Money Luxury, we trace how a Navy carrier pilot turned Cadillac salesman became the founder of the most valuable family-held rental fleet in the world — a global operation of more than 2 million vehicles across more than 10,000 locations, still 100 percent privately held under Taylor family ownership almost 70 years after seven cars were parked in a St. Louis dealership basement.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

We open on Enterprise Holdings today — the parent company behind Enterprise Rent-A-Car, National Car Rental, and Alamo, with over $35 billion in annual revenue, more than 90,000 employees, more than 10,000 offices worldwide, and the largest fleet of rental vehicles ever assembled under a single private owner.

We trace the family's ancestral origins in the American Midwest — the Taylor line, the St. Louis mercantile world, and the aviator's childhood that pushed Jack Taylor toward the deck of a Yorktown-class carrier the year he turned 22.

We follow Jack C. Taylor through his early life — Washington University in St. Louis, the wartime enlistment in Naval Aviation, the Hellcat squadron in the Pacific, the Navy Air Medal, and the 1945 return to a country that no longer required combat pilots.

We watch him arrive on the showroom floor at Arthur Lindburg's Cadillac dealership on Natural Bridge Road — 11 years selling cars, the customers who kept asking about longer-term leasing, and the 1957 conversation that produced Executive Leasing with seven cars in the basement and a 25 percent stake personally underwritten by his employer.

We reconstruct the pivot from leasing to daily rental in 1962 — the insurance-replacement niche that no national competitor had bothered to occupy, the neighborhood office footprint away from airports, the free customer pickup, and the operating model that Hertz and Avis would spend the next 30 years trying to catch up to.

We trace the 1969 rebrand to Enterprise Rent-A-Car after the aircraft carrier that had carried Jack Taylor across the Pacific, and the deliberate refusal to compete on airport counters — the geography, the customer, and the pricing that let Enterprise grow underneath the industry's radar for nearly two decades.

We follow the second generation into the executive suite — Andy Taylor's rise from local branch manager to chief executive in 1991, the succession Jack engineered with the patience of a man who intended his company to outlast him, and the family-first management philosophy Warren Buffett publicly identified as the model for the ideal American family business.

We trace the peak-power years — the acquisitions of National Car Rental and Alamo in 2007, the consolidation into Enterprise Holdings, the industry-leading market share, and the private-ownership structure that let the family invest through recessions the public competitors could not survive.



We watch the third generation take control — Chrissy Taylor's rise to chief executive of Enterprise Holdings in 2020, the granddaughter of the Cadillac salesman now running the largest privately held rental fleet in the world, and the ownership structure Jack Taylor engineered to keep his descendants in the building.

And we close on the founder's death in July 2016 at the age of 94 — the seven cars in the basement in 1957, the 2 million vehicles on the road at the end, the personal exemplar Warren Buffett kept returning to whenever he was asked what an American family business could look like when the family actually refused to sell, and the single decision — never go public — that made every other decision possible.

snippet.title: The Dark Origins of America's Greatest Art Collection
snippet.description:
Inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the name Havemeyer appears on the wall labels beside some of the greatest paintings in the world. There is El Greco's View of Toledo. There are 14 works by Edgar Degas. At its height the collection held as many as six Rembrandts, a Goya, a Velázquez, and nearly 2,000 objects ranked among the finest ever assembled in America. What the labels never explain is where the money came from. It came from a sugar monopoly that controlled 98 percent of the American market, from immigrant workers who fainted in groups of hundreds inside a Brooklyn refinery, from senators who bought sugar stock before they voted on the sugar tariff, and from a customs fraud that a sitting President called the most colossal ever perpetrated against his government. At the center of it stood Henry Osborne Havemeyer, the Sugar King, and a thin strip of corset metal that the museum will never hang on its walls.

In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the Havemeyer fortune behind the H.O. Havemeyer Collection at the Met — from a Brooklyn refining family that took over the American sugar market in a single decade, through the senatorial bribery of the 1894 tariff debates and the customs fraud uncovered on Pier 24 in 1907, to the Fifth Avenue mansion of Louis Comfort Tiffany interiors where Louisine Havemeyer assembled one of the great private collections in American history with money the law had every reason to take back.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

We open on Pier 24 at the Williamsburg refinery on November 20, 1907 — Customs Special Agent Richard Parr, the platform scale, the small flat spring of corset steel pulled from a hole drilled into the wooden platform, and the $100,000 cash bribe a dock superintendent offered him within hours to forget what he had found.

We trace the corset-steel scheme — the precise mechanism by which the American Sugar Refining Company had been underpaying duty on every pound of raw sugar landed in Brooklyn for years, the federal indictments, and the death of Henry Osborne Havemeyer of heart failure two weeks later at the age of 60.

We follow the founder back to his beginnings — Frederick C. Havemeyer's Brooklyn refinery on Vandam Street in 1807, the family's vertical integration of the East River waterfront, and the boy who fought his principal at school and never stopped fighting anyone who stood between him and a market.

We trace the building of the trust — the 1887 consolidation of the Sugar Refineries Company, the 98 percent monopoly on American sugar refining capacity by the early 1890s, and Henry Havemeyer's testimony before the United States Industrial Commission in 1899: "the mother of all trusts is the Customs Tariff Bill."

We reconstruct the 1894 tariff fight — the eight U.S. senators who admitted under oath to having bought sugar stock before voting on the sugar tariff, the 600 amendments to the Wilson-Gorman Tariff Act, and the trust's open purchase of the legislative process in broad daylight.

We follow E. C. Knight to the Supreme Court — the 1895 decision that ruled that controlling 98 percent of a national industry was not a federal antitrust violation, on the theory that "manufacturing is local," and the doctrine that effectively neutered the Sherman Antitrust Act for the next fifteen years.

We step inside the Brooklyn refinery floor — the immigrant workers fainting in groups of hundreds in lethal heat, the wages, the injuries, the deaths, and the human cost embedded in every pound of refined sugar that left the Williamsburg waterfront.

snippet.title: The "Old Money" Dynasty Who Survived Napoleon and Hitler: The Wendels
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the 322-year story of the de Wendel family — a Lorraine dynasty that bought a derelict ironworks in 1704 for 9,621 livres and spent the next twelve generations turning it into one of the longest-running industrial empires in European history, surviving the French Revolution, the Napoleonic Wars, two German annexations, two World Wars, Nazi confiscation, socialist nationalization, and the collapse of European steel — and emerging in the twenty-first century as a Euronext-listed investment platform managing nearly €47 billion in third-party assets, still controlled by roughly 1,200 family shareholders, with a Humbert de Wendel still seated on the supervisory board.

————————————————————————————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

————————————————————————————————————————

On March 26, 1704, a minor Lorraine nobleman named Jean-Martin de Wendel paid the equivalent of forty-eight years of a craftsman's wages for a derelict forge at Hayange in the Moselle Valley — a furnace, a hammer mill, and a cutting mill that the previous owner had failed to make profitable.

Within three decades, Jean-Martin had grown the operation seventy-three-fold by recognizing what no one else had: the valley combined charcoal-rich woodland, hydraulic power from the Fensch stream, abundant iron ore, and a royal artillery works at Thionville desperate for a reliable supplier of cannonballs.

When the French Revolution confiscated the forge, the family matriarch Marguerite d'Hayange sold cannonballs to the same revolutionary government that had imprisoned her — because she understood that usefulness was the only protection a noble family possessed during the Terror.

Napoleon returned the forge in 1804, financed by the Seillière bank — a name that would resurface two centuries later when a Seillière descendant rebuilt the family fortune from scratch.

The Franco-Prussian War of 1871 cut Lorraine in half, placing Hayange inside the newly annexed German territory while the family's French operations remained on the other side of a hostile border — and the de Wendels did the only thing that made sense: they ran both halves simultaneously, becoming arguably the only industrial family in Europe operating openly in two countries at war with each other.

François de Wendel served twenty-two years as president of the Comité des forges, the most powerful industrial lobby in France, while also running a steel plant he could not legally visit on the German side of the border.

When the Nazis annexed Lorraine in 1940, they expelled the family and confiscated the works, and the de Wendel, who joined the Resistance, was tortured in an SS camp before the Liberation returned the assets in 1945.

In 1977, the family saw the nationalization of French steel coming seven months before it arrived and moved everything of value out of the structure the Mitterrand government was about to seize — transferring the wealth into a holding company called CGIP that would become the seed of the modern Wendel Group.

The architect of the modern transformation was Ernest-Antoine Seillière, who turned CGIP into a disciplined private-equity-style platform, then merged it with the sister entity Marine-Wendel in 2002 to create Wendel Investissement — a restructuring that required a unanimous vote from approximately 400 family shareholders dispersed across multiple generations.

That same year, Wendel partnered with KKR on a €3.6 billion leveraged buyout of Legrand, one of the largest LBO transactions in European history, followed by an activist 21.5 percent stake in Saint-Gobain — announcing that the family intended to compete at the top tier of European investment, not passively hold inherited stakes.

Today, the family holding entity Wendel-Participations SE is owned by approximately 1,200 members of the Wendel family and controls about 39.3 percent of the group's share capital — a governance structure that has held together through three centuries of catastrophe.

This is the story of a single family that learned, across twelve generations, that the form of wealth must change at every generation, but the conviction to rebuild does not — and that when everyone else sees wreckage, the ore is still underneath.

snippet.title: The Real Family Behind "There Will Be Blood": The Dark History of the Doheny Oil Dynasty
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the true Gilded Age oil dynasty behind Daniel Day-Lewis's Daniel Plainview in "There Will Be Blood" — Edward Laurence Doheny, the broke Irish-American prospector who borrowed four hundred dollars, sharpened a eucalyptus trunk to a point, and drove it into the ground in Echo Park in 1892 to start the Los Angeles oil boom. From a parking lot at Colton Street to the largest single oil well in history at Cerro Azul Number Four, from the hundred thousand dollar bribe in a black leather bag carried to Albert Fall's room at the Wardman Park Hotel to the warm gun under Hugh Plunkett's body at Greystone Mansion, this is the dynastic autopsy of the family Upton Sinclair fictionalized in "Oil!" and Paul Thomas Anderson resurrected on film.

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------

Born August 10, 1856 in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin, Edward Doheny spent seventeen years failing as a prospector across South Dakota, Arizona, and New Mexico before arriving in Los Angeles in 1891, broke and unable to pay his boarding-house bill.

In 1892 he saw a teamster's wagon dripping tar near Echo Park, borrowed $400 from his partner Charles Canfield, and dug a six-by-four-foot shaft by hand near Colton and Patton Streets. The well struck oil at 155 feet at 40 barrels a day.

By 1896 he was a millionaire. By 1920 his Mexican operations in the Huasteca were the largest in the world's largest oil-producing country. Cerro Azul Number Four blew in February 1916 at 260,858 barrels per day, audible 16 miles away — still the highest single-well rate in oil history.

By 1925 his net worth had crossed $100 million, making him richer than John D. Rockefeller. He sold the controlling interest in Pan American Petroleum to Standard Oil of Indiana for $38 million that same year.

In November 1921, Secretary of the Interior Albert Fall — a former Kingston, New Mexico prospecting acquaintance — phoned Doheny to receive a hundred thousand dollar "loan." Doheny's son Ned Junior and Ned's secretary Hugh Plunkett carried the cash in a black leather bag to the Wardman Park Hotel in Washington. Fall counted the bills and signed a promissory note.

Fall was convicted in October 1929, the first cabinet member ever convicted of a felony in office. Five months later, on identical evidence, Doheny was acquitted in one hour. Senator Heflin's verdict on the verdict: "You can't convict a million dollars."

On February 16, 1929, four months after the family moved into Greystone, the most expensive house in Beverly Hills at $3,166,578, Ned Doheny Junior was found shot above his left ear in a green silk dressing gown. Hugh Plunkett lay face-down in the anteroom, a Bisley Colt under his body, a cigarette burned into the skin of his fingers.

Detective Leslie T. White arrived three hours after the shots and found the gun still warm, every fingerprint wiped clean, no powder burns on Plunkett's skull, and the property already secured by Doheny family private detectives before the police were called. The case was closed in 36 hours. No inquest. No autopsy.

Doheny's second wife Estelle — the former telephone operator he married three months after his divorce — became a Papal Countess, secretly went blind, hired readers, and became the first woman to privately purchase a Gutenberg Bible in 1950 for $70,000. The Archdiocese of Los Angeles auctioned her collection in 1987 for $37.8 million.

Upton Sinclair published "Oil!" in 1927, transparently fictionalizing Doheny as J. Arnold Ross. Eighty years later, Paul Thomas Anderson built "There Will Be Blood" on its bones. Daniel Day-Lewis filmed the final bowling alley scene at the actual Greystone Mansion where Ned and Hugh died.

The site of the original 1892 well at Echo Park is now a parking lot serving the public swimming pool at 1419 Colton Street. There is no marker. There is no plaque.

Hugh Plunkett lay face-down in the anteroom, a Bisley Colt under his body, a cigarette burned into the skin of his fingers.

Doheny's second wife Estelle — the former telephone operator he married three months after his divorce — became a Papal Countess, secretly went blind, hired readers, and became the first woman to privately purchase a Gutenberg Bible in 1950 for $70,000. The Archdiocese of Los Angeles auctioned her collection in 1987 for $37.8 million.

Upton Sinclair published "Oil!" in 1927, transparently fictionalizing Doheny as J. Arnold Ross. Eighty years later, Paul Thomas Anderson built "There Will Be Blood" on its bones. Daniel Day-Lewis filmed the final bowling alley scene at the actual Greystone Mansion where Ned and Hugh died.

snippet.description:
On the night of October seventh, nineteen sixty six, a rented station wagon broke through the iron gates of Rough Point in Newport, Rhode Island, and crushed the man who had just stepped out of it to open them. The Newport police took seventy two hours to call it an accident. They never gave her a sobriety test. They never convened a grand jury. And for the next twenty seven years, the woman who killed Eduardo Tirella was never asked a single hard question about that night.

In this video, we tell the full story of Doris Duke, the twelve year old who inherited one hundred million dollars from her tobacco baron father Buck Duke in October nineteen twenty five and was christened by the press the richest little girl in the world. 

We follow her cold Brearley childhood under her mother Nanaline, her nineteen thirty debut at Rough Point, her first marriage in nineteen thirty five to the ambitious senate candidate Jimmy Cromwell and his one and a half million dollar nineteen forty three Reno divorce, the seven acre Honolulu palace Shangri La she built for one and four tenths million dollars and filled with three thousand five hundred objects of Islamic art, her surfing friendship with the Olympic swimmer Duke Kahanamoku, the catastrophic loss of her premature daughter Arden in July nineteen forty, her wartime work in Cairo and Rome and her rumoured Cairo affair with General George S. Patton, her nineteen forty seven Paris marriage to the Dominican playboy Porfirio Rubirosa and the thirteen month settlement paid in polo ponies, Ferraris, a converted B twenty five bomber, and a Paris townhouse, 

the six year working friendship with the set designer Eduardo Tirella and the September nineteen sixty six conversation in which he told her he was leaving her employ, the killing at the Rough Point gates on the seventh of October nineteen sixty six and the seventy two hour Newport police accident finding, the two hundred and one thousand dollar nineteen seventy four civil settlement with the Tirella family, the arrival of the Irish butler Bernard Lafferty in her household in nineteen eighty seven and his takeover of her schedule, her medications, and the April nineteen ninety three will, the darkened bedroom at Falcon Lair in October nineteen ninety three and the morphine drip her butler controlled, the nineteen ninety five Los Angeles district attorney's inquiry that closed without charges, 

the nineteen ninety six probate settlement that paid her disinherited adopted daughter Chandi Heffner sixty five million dollars, and the Vanity Fair investigation by Peter Lance that, in October two thousand and twenty, led Newport Police Chief Gary Silva to publicly admit that the Tirella killing today would be treated as a homicide. 

We close with the verdict of the Duke fortune: a charitable foundation that has distributed more than two billion dollars in grants since nineteen ninety three, three world class institutions built on what survived her, and a small marble headstone in a Dover, New Jersey cemetery that bears the name of a man whose sister waited fifty four years to be told what she had always known.

snippet.title: The Failed Baseball Player Who Built The $7 Billion: Little Caesars Empire
snippet.description:
A knee injury in the minor leagues ended Mike Ilitch's baseball career in 1955. He was a career .280 hitter across four seasons in the farm systems of the Detroit Tigers, the New York Yankees, and the Washington Senators — good enough to play 336 professional games, never good enough to receive the call to the majors. He sold awnings door-to-door after that, then insurance, then scraped together $10,000 with his wife Marian to open a pizza shop in a Detroit suburb in 1959. Thirty-three years later, he bought the Detroit Tigers — the same franchise whose minor league system had sent him home with a bad knee — and the black-and-white photograph of a young Mike Ilitch in his Tigers uniform hung in the owner's suite at Comerica Park for the rest of his life.
--------------------

--------------------

Michael Ilitch Sr. was born on July 20, 1929, in Detroit, to Macedonian immigrants who had arrived in 1924. He played shortstop at Cooley High School and was named All-City in both baseball and track. Upon graduating in 1947, the Detroit Tigers offered him a minor league contract — but he joined the United States Marine Corps instead, serving four years and attaining the rank of Sergeant.

When he returned to Detroit in 1952, the Tigers honored their earlier interest. He carved out a career as a professional infielder across the Tigers, Yankees, and Senators farm systems — batting .324 with a .375 on-base percentage in 1954, his finest season. The knee injury that ended his career in 1955 came at twenty-six.

On a blind date arranged by his father in 1954, Mike met Marian Bayoff, who had grown up working in her father's restaurant. They married shortly after meeting. By 1959 they had assembled roughly $10,000 in personal savings and borrowed an additional $15,000. Mike wanted to call the restaurant "Pizza Treat" or "Pizza Cheap." Marian called her husband her "Little Caesar," and insisted the restaurant carry that name.

On May 8, 1959, Mike and Marian Ilitch opened Little Caesars Pizza Treat in a strip mall at 32594 Cherry Hill Road in Garden City, Michigan. The shop moved roughly 296 pizzas in its opening week. The Ilitches began franchising in 1962. In 1971, the chain moved to a carry-out-only model. In 1979, the "Pizza! Pizza!" two-for-one campaign launched and ran continuously for nineteen years.
In 1982, Mike Ilitch bought the Detroit Red Wings — nicknamed the "Dead Wings" — for $8 million, funding the $1 million down payment from advance season-ticket sales collected after the deal was signed. The Red Wings won the Stanley Cup in 1997, ending a 42-year championship drought, then again in 1998, 2002, and 2008.

In 1987, Ilitch purchased the historic Fox Theatre and undertook a $12.5 million renovation. He moved Little Caesars' corporate headquarters into the adjacent offices — the first time a major corporate headquarters had relocated to downtown Detroit in twenty-seven years.
In 1992, when the Detroit Tigers were put up for sale by Tom Monaghan — founder of Domino's Pizza — Mike Ilitch bought the franchise for approximately $85 million. The Tigers won four consecutive AL Central Division Championships from 2011 to 2014.

In 2004, Little Caesars permanently launched the Hot-N-Ready model: a large pepperoni pizza, ready to go, for five dollars. From 2008 to 2015, it became the fastest-growing pizza chain in the United States.

After Rosa Parks was robbed and assaulted in her Detroit home in 1994 at age 81, Mike Ilitch quietly called and offered to pay her rent for as long as she needed. He wrote a check every month until her death in 2005, without ever seeking publicity.
Mike Ilitch died on February 10, 2017, at eighty-seven. Marian Ilitch — named by Forbes in 2025 as the third-wealthiest self-made woman in the United States with an estimated net worth of $6.9 billion — sat atop the empire at ninety years old.

In this in-depth, full-length documentary compilation, we explore the country estates, private asylums, and locked wings where the British royal family quietly hid the relatives whose existence threatened the myth of an unblemished bloodline — the cousins, sisters, and uncles erased from family trees, removed from official portraits, and consigned to comfortable prisons until the day they died.

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------

Monarchy depends on the appearance of perfection — bloodlines free of weakness, families free of the illnesses that visit everyone else. When reality refused to cooperate, royal families had a choice: acknowledge the truth, or make the problem disappear.

Wealth made disappearance possible. Private institutions. Country estates converted to medical facilities. Staff bound by contracts carrying penalties severe enough to guarantee silence. Records sealed, altered, or destroyed entirely.

The relatives buried this way spent years or decades in comfortable prisons, denied not freedom exactly but acknowledgment — their names removed from family trees, their photographs excluded from official portraits, their very existence a secret maintained by people paid to forget they had ever met them.

This compilation walks through the houses where the British royal family hid its inconvenient relatives, and whether the people they erased ever understood why their own families had decided to disappear them.
